title: Diphenhydramine
wiki_lead:
Diphenhydramine, or Diphenylhydramine, sold under the brand name Benadryl among others, is an antihistamine and sedative. Although generally considered sedating, diphenhydramine can cause paradoxical central nervous system stimulation in some individuals, particularly at higher doses. This may manifest as agitation, anxiety, or restlessness rather than sedation. It is a first-generation H1-antihistamine (i.e. it blocks histamine) with sedative effects. Diphenhydramine is also a potent anticholinergic. It is mainly used to treat allergies, insomnia, and symptoms of the common cold. It is also less commonly used for tremors in parkinsonism, and nausea. It is taken by mouth, injected into a vein, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin. Maximal effect is typically around two hours after an oral dose, and effects can last for up to seven hours.
Common side effects include sleepiness, poor coordination, and an upset stomach. There is no clear risk of harm when used during pregnancy; however, use during breastfeeding is not recommended.
It was developed by George Rieveschl and put into commercial use in 1946. It is available as a generic medication. In 2023, it was the 294th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 700,000 prescriptions.
Its sedative and deliriant effects have led to some cases of recreational use.

Medical uses

Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine used to treat several conditions including allergic symptoms and itchiness, the common cold, insomnia, motion sickness, and extrapyramidal symptoms. Diphenhydramine also has local anesthetic properties, and has been used as such in people allergic to common local anesthetics such as lidocaine.


Allergies
Diphenhydramine is effective in the treatment of allergies. As of 2007, it was the most commonly used antihistamine for acute allergic reactions in the emergency department.
By injection, it is often used in addition to epinephrine for anaphylaxis, although as of 2007 its use for this purpose had not been properly studied. Its use is only recommended once acute symptoms have improved.

Topical formulations of diphenhydramine are available, including creams, lotions, gels, sprays, and eye drops. These are used to relieve itching and have the advantage of causing fewer systemic effects (such as drowsiness) than oral forms.


Movement disorders
Diphenhydramine is used to treat parkinsonism. It is also used to treat acute dystonia, including torticollis and oculogyric crisis caused by typical antipsychotics.


Sleep
Because of its sedative properties, diphenhydramine is widely used in nonprescription sleep aids for insomnia. The drug is an ingredient in several products sold as sleep aids. Diphenhydramine can cause minor psychological dependence. Diphenhydramine has also been used as an anxiolytic.
Diphenhydramine has been used off-label by parents in an attempt to make their children sleep and to sedate them on long-distance flights. This
grok_lead: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1 receptor antagonist and antihistamine medication that is widely used to relieve symptoms of allergic reactions, such as sneezing, runny nose, itchy eyes, and hives, as well as to treat motion sickness, insomnia, and certain extrapyramidal symptoms. Originally approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1946 as a prescription drug under the brand name Benadryl, which includes formulations such as softgel capsules (e.g., Liqui-Gels) designed to be swallowed whole to avoid the bitter taste of the liquid contents if the capsule breaks in the mouth, it became available over-the-counter in the 1980s and remains one of the most commonly used antihistamines worldwide due to its broad efficacy and accessibility. As an ethanolamine derivative, diphenhydramine exerts its primary therapeutic effects by competitively blocking histamine H1 receptors, thereby inhibiting the allergic response mediated by histamine release, while also crossing the blood-brain barrier to produce sedative properties that contribute to its use as a short-term sleep aid in adults. It additionally possesses anticholinergic, antimuscarinic, and local anesthetic properties due to its inhibition of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and sodium channel blockade, which can enhance its utility in conditions like vertigo, nausea, and acute dystonias but also increase the risk of adverse effects. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly absorbed after oral administration with a bioavailability of 40-72%, reaching peak plasma concentrations in 2-3 hours, and has an elimination half-life of approximately 2.4-9.3 hours, primarily metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes such as CYP2D6. Common side effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and blurred vision, which are largely attributable to its central nervous system penetration and anticholinergic activity, while more serious risks involve QT interval prolongation, seizures, and cardiovascular toxicity, particularly in overdose or high-dose misuse. The FDA has issued warnings about the dangers of high doses, which can lead to hallucinations, seizures, coma, or death, especially when abused for recreational purposes or in combination with other sedative s. Due to these sedative effects and potential for tolerance, diphenhydramine is not recommended for long-term use in treating insomnia, and caution is advised in children under 6 years, particularly as it is not recommended for infants under 1 year of age and should only be used in children under 2 years under medical supervision due to risks such as excessive drowsiness, breathing problems, and other side effects, older adults, and individuals with conditions like glaucoma, asthma, or prostate enlargement. In 2025, expert reviews have called for phasing out diphenhydramine from over-the-counter availability due to its risks outweighing benefits, amid reports of an 87% increase in pediatric poisonings over the past decade and elevated delirium risks in hospitalized older adults. Despite its long-standing role in allergy management, newer second-generation antihistamines are often preferred for their reduced sedation, though diphenhydramine continues to serve as an essential adjunct in acute settings like anaphylaxis treatment.
